title: Loop and pole: ط ظ

bigIdea.text: ط (ṭa) and ظ (ẓa) share one body: an oval loop with a tall upright stroke. Both are heavy. No dot = ṭa, a heavy 't'. One dot = ẓa, a heavy 'th' as in 'this'.

proper.text: The loop sits on the line and a tall stroke stands up from it. ظ has one dot beside the stroke, above the loop. Their shape hardly changes at the start, middle or end of a word, and they have no tail below the line.

Sounds: ط is a heavy 't'. The tongue touches where it does for ت, but the back of the tongue rises and the tongue presses up, so the sound is deep, with no puff of air after it. ظ is a heavy 'th' as in 'this': the tongue meets the edges of the upper front teeth as for ذ, with the back of the tongue raised.

Sifat: both are 'raised' (isti'la) and 'closed' (itbaq), and both hold the breath back (jahr). ط is 'strong' (shiddah: its sound stops fully) and bounces with a sukun (qalqalah). ظ is 'soft' (rakhawa: its sound flows).

proper.text: Heavy or light: both are heavy. They are two of the seven heavy letters (خ ص ض غ ط ق ظ).

Common mistakes. Persian/Urdu readers: ط is read like ت, and ظ like 'z' (ز). English speakers: ط comes out as a light English 't' with a puff of air, and ظ as a light 'th' or as 'z'. Fix: raise the back of the tongue first, then say the letter.

points.detail: Tongue against the roots of the upper front teeth (shared with ت and د)
Tongue against the edges of the upper front teeth (shared with ث and ذ)

memoryHook.text: Loop and pole means heavy: ṭa is a heavy t, ẓa a heavy 'th'.

extras.text: Linguists describe Arabic ت and ك as said with a puff of air (aspirated), and ط and ق without one.
Of the 28 letters, ظ is the rarest in the app's Quran text: 853 times (hamza counted together with its seats).

tip.text: ط stops: the tongue presses at the roots of the upper front teeth, then releases. ظ flows: the tongue meets the edges of the upper teeth and the voice keeps going. Keep both heavy.

questions.q: Which letter is a loop with a tall stroke and one dot?
explain: Right: loop, pole and a dot is ẓa.
ṭa is the same body with no dot.
ḍad has a loop and a dot, but a small tooth instead of the tall stroke.
kaf is tall, but it has no loop and no dot.

questions.q: Are ط and ظ heavy or light?
explain: Right: both are among the seven heavy letters.
Neither is light.
ẓa is heavy too.
ṭa is heavy too.

questions.q: Which letter of this pair bounces (qalqalah) when it has a sukun?
explain: Right: ṭa is one of the five qalqalah letters (ق ط ب ج د).
ẓa is not a qalqalah letter.
Only ṭa bounces.
ṭa does bounce.

fa and qaf have a small round head.

questions.q: Linguists describe which of these Arabic letters as said WITHOUT a puff of air?
explain: Right: ṭa (like qaf) has no puff of air.
ta is described with a puff of air (aspirated).
kaf is described with a puff of air (aspirated).
Only ṭa is unaspirated here.

questions.q: Your ط sounds like an English 't'. What fixes it?
options: Raise the back of the tongue and press the tongue up, with no puff of air
Move the tongue to the edges of the teeth
explain: Right: that gives the heavy ṭa.
That makes a 'th'-type sound (ث ذ ظ).
A hum is not part of ṭa.
The lips are not used for ṭa.

questions.q: Which letter is the heavy partner of ذ (same place, back of the tongue raised)?
explain: Right: ẓa shares dhal's place but is heavy.
ṭa shares the place of ت and د.
ḍad has its own place along the side of the tongue.
zay is a light letter with a whistle.

questions.q: At the start, middle and end of a word, the shapes of ط and ظ…
options: …hardly change, and never drop below the line
…lose the tall stroke in the middle
…grow a tail below the line at the end
explain: Right: loop and pole stay the same.
The stroke stays.
They have no tail below the line.
ẓa keeps its dot everywhere.
